3 | P a g e
Judgment
1. This appeal arises from the judgment and sentence dated 18.01.2018, delivered by the
learned High Court Judge of Colombo. The Accused-Appellant (hereinafter referred to
as “the Appellant”) was indicted before the High Court of Colombo for committing the
offence of criminal breach of trust, an offence punishable under Section 389 of the
Penal Code.
2. At the conclusion of the trial, the learned High Court Judge found the Appellant guilty
of the charge and convicted him accordingly. Consequently, the Appellant was
sentenced to three years’ rigorous imprisonment and ordered to pay a fine of Rs.
500,000.00, with a default sentence of nine months’ imprisonment. The learned Trial
Judge further ordered the Appellant to pay Rs. 9 million as compensation to PW1, with
a default sentence of eighteen months’ imprisonment.
3. It is against the said conviction and sentence that the Appellant has preferred the instant
appeal.
4. The Appellant has urged the following grounds of appeal;
a. The Accused-Appellant denied the opportunity of a fair trial in the High Court;
b. The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the legal principle of
estoppel which is applicable to the main prosecution witness, in his judgment;
c. The Learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself regarding the principles
embodied in Chapter vii of the Evidence Ordinance, especially Section 93 of
the said Ordinance; and
d. The Learned High Court Judge has failed to apply the test of probability to the
stand taken by the main prosecution witness that the Accused-Appellant, being
an Attorney-at-Law of a relatively long standing, will devote his time to projects
without remuneration for a period of two years only on reimbursement of
expenses.
5. The amount involved in the charge of criminal breach of trust was AUD 108,500.00.
The prosecution case is that the said amount was credited to NRFC Account No.
4 | P a g e
9393462 for the purpose of investing in Hakwatuna Oya Resorts Pvt Ltd. It is alleged
that the Appellant thereafter dishonestly misappropriated or converted the said funds to
his own use, in violation of the terms of the express or implied legal arrangement
between the Appellant and PW1.
6. At the trial, 11 witnesses testified for the prosecution. The Appellant made a dock
statement and did not call any witness to testify.
7. The Appellant has maintained that the monies in question were received by him as
professional fees for the services rendered by him to the said company and, accordingly,
contends that he was entitled to utilize those monies at his discretion.
8. The principal contention advanced by the Appellant was that the Accused-Appellant,
being an Attorney-at-Law of a relatively long standing, would devote his time to
projects without remuneration for a period of two years only on reimbursement of
expenses. So, his argument was that such monies were used as his professional fee for
the services he provided for the said company.
9. Section 388 of the Penal Code provides for the offence of criminal breach of trust.
10. Section 388 of the Penal Code reads as follows:
Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over
property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or
dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law
prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, or of any legal contract,
express or implied, which he has made touching the discharge of such trust, or willfully
suffers any other person so to do, commits 'criminal breach of trust.'
11. In this regard, it would be appropriate to consider the ingredients necessary to prove
criminal breach of trust as follows;
a. Entrustment with property or dominion over property, and either
b. (i). Dishonest misappropriation or conversion to his own use, or
5 | P a g e
(ii). Dishonest use or disposal, or
(iii). Willfully suffering any other to do b (i) or b (ii)
12. Those being the ingredients necessary to prove the offence of criminal breach of trust,
the entrustment of property is undisputed as per the prosecution witnesses.
13. PW1, Nihal Pallege Nanayakkara, was the first witness to testify for the prosecution.
He is a consultant physician who, after working at several hospitals in Sri Lanka,
migrated to Australia with his wife. According to his evidence, he subsequently formed
an intention to invest in a hotel resort project in Sri Lanka. While working in Sri Lanka,
PW1 became acquainted with one Sumathipala Kariyawasam, a bank employee, and
subsequently came to know the Accused-Appellant through him.
14. Following several discussions concerning the proposed investment, PW1 decided to
name the proposed hotel “Hakwatuna Oya Resorts.” He thereafter caused the business
to be incorporated as a company under the name of ‘Hakwatuna Oya Resorts Pvt Ltd,’
with himself and his wife being registered as its directors. PW1 further appointed
Sumathipala Kariyawasam and the Accused-Appellant as alternative directors of the
said company. In addition, PW1 established another company under the name “Nilaweli
Beach Resorts and Spa,” in which he and his wife were appointed as directors, while
other persons were appointed as alternative directors.
15. In furtherance of the proposed hotel project, PW1, on several occasions, remitted funds
from his wife’s account maintained at the Australian ANZ Bank to his NRFC Account
maintained at the People’s Bank in Sri Lanka. At the request of the Accused-Appellant
and Kariyawasam, PW1 subsequently executed a power of attorney authorizing them
to operate and deal with the funds maintained in the said NRFC account for the purpose
of making investments in and meeting expenses relating to the proposed hotel project.
16. By virtue of the authority conferred upon them under the said power of attorney, the
Accused-Appellant and Kariyawasam thereby obtained control over the funds
deposited into PW1’s NRFC account. PW1’s evidence was that he had expressly
instructed them that the monies placed at their disposal were to be utilized solely for
the purposes connected with the proposed hotel investment.
6 | P a g e
“ප්‍ර: ඒ කාරණය හැර, හහාහෙල් ව්‍යාපෘති සදහා මුදල් වියදම් කිරීම හැර හව්‍නත් කාරණා
සදහා මුදල් වියදම් කිරීමෙ ඔබ කිසියම් අව්‍ස්ථාව්‍ක කාරියව්‍සම්ෙ හහෝ හම් විත්තිකරුෙ
උපහදස් දීල තිබුනද?
උ: නැහැ.
ප්‍ර: එහ ාහකාෙ ඔබ කිව්ව්‍ා ඔබහේ අව්‍හබෝධය තිබුහේ ඒ මුදල් හහෝෙල් ව්‍යාපෘතිය සදහා
පමණක් වියදම් කරේන කියල?
උ: ඔව්.” (at vide page 23 of the Appeal Brief)
17. In 2009 August or September, PW1 caused Sumathipala Kariyawasam to resign from
his position as an alternative director of the said company. PW1 testified that he had
taken this step upon discovering that Kariyawasam had, by utilizing the authority
conferred upon him under the power of attorney, dealt with or appropriated assets
amounting to approximately 10% of PW1’s estate and that irregularities and other
malpractices had occurred in the affairs of the company. Thereafter, PW1 caused audits
to be conducted in respect of all his business entities and appointed one Gothama
Hewawitharana (PW2) as the new alternative director of the company.
18. Following his resignation as an alternative director, Kariyawasam ceased to have any
further involvement in or dealings with Hakwatuna Oya Resorts Pvt Ltd.
19. According to the testimony of PW1, the land intended for the Hakwatuna Oya Resorts
project was acquired in two separate transactions. The first portion, comprising
approximately one-half of the land, was purchased in the early part of 2009 for a sum
of Rs. 6 million, during the period in which Kariyawasam was associated with the
company. The remaining portion was subsequently purchased after PW2 had assumed
the position of alternative director.
20. It is significant that, according to PW1, he had not made any payments to either the
Accused-Appellant or PW2 by way of salary or professional fees. Further, PW1
testified that there was no agreement or other arrangement between himself and the
Accused-Appellant pursuant to which the latter was entitled to receive any such
payment.
7 | P a g e
“ප්‍ර: ඒ ඇහරේන ඔබ හගෝ ම හහ්ව්‍ාවි ාරණ සමග හහෝ හම් විත්තිකරු ව්‍න මහනෝජ්
දිසානායකෙ යම්කිසි පඩියක් දීහම් එකගත්ව්‍ක් තිබුනද?
උ: නැහැ.
ප්‍ර: ඔවුේ කල හස්ව්‍ාව්‍ හව්‍නුහව්‍ේ හව්‍ේ හව්‍ේ ව්‍ශහයේ මුදල් හගවීහම් එකග ාව්‍ක්
තිබුනද?
උ: නැ .
ප්‍ර: නානායක්කාර මහ ා කිසිම අව්‍ස්ථාව්‍ක හමම මහනෝජ් දිසානායක කියන විත්තිකරු
හම් සමාගහම් උපහේශක හස්ව්‍ාව්‍ක් හැටියෙ මුදල් හගවීහම් එකග ාව්‍ක් තිබුනද?
උ: නැහැ.” (at vide pages 16-17 of the Appeal Brief)
21. Contrary to the foregoing, however, there was an agreement between PW1, the
Accused-Appellant, and PW2 whereby the Accused-Appellant and PW2 were to be
entitled to 7% and 3%, respectively, of the shares of the hotel project. According to the
said arrangement, such shares were to be granted in consideration of their undertaking
to attend to and supervise all matters relating to the construction of the hotel, and for
no other purpose.
22. The office of Hakwatuna Oya Resorts Pvt Ltd. was situated at an address in Colombo
5, and the monthly rental in respect of the premises was paid by PW1. Further, at the
request of the Accused-Appellant, PW1’s funds were utilized for the purchase of a
Prado vehicle. The Company also employed two workers, whose salaries were paid out
of the funds of the company.
23. There were also instances in which PW1, at the request of the Accused-Appellant,
deposited monies into the personal bank accounts of the Accused-Appellant and PW2.
According to PW1, such monies were remitted strictly for the purpose of being utilized
in connection with the hotel investment. PW1 further testified that the Accused-
Appellant had informed him that, if a 7% share in the project were transferred to them,
a tax of 7% would become payable. Accordingly, instead of transferring the said 7%
share, PW1 was requested to deposit the relevant monies into their personal bank
accounts for the purpose of investment in the hotel project.
8 | P a g e
24. PW1 further testified that, following the withdrawal of Kariyawasam from the affairs
of the company, both the Accused-Appellant and PW2 were authorized to withdraw
monies from PW1’s personal account maintained at the People’s Bank, Subject to a
limit of Rs. 200,000.
25. PW1 categorically testified that, on five separate occasions, he deposited a total sum of
AUD 108,500 into the personal bank account of the Accused-Appellant. He further
testified that a sum of AUD 46,500 was deposited into the personal bank account of
PW2 for the purpose of investing in the said hotel project.
26. PW1 further testified that he received five vouchers in respect of these transactions and
that, on each occasion, he signed the relevant voucher and forwarded it to the Accused-
Appellant. At a subsequent stage, PW2 informed PW1 that the Accused-Appellant had
prevented him from entering the office premises and from attending to the work relating
to the company.
27. In those circumstances, PW1 requested an audit be conducted into the affairs of the
company and that a meeting be convened on 19.10.2010. The Accused-Appellant,
however, did not attend the said meeting. Thereafter, PW1, together with his wife, PW2,
PW5, and two other Attorneys-at-Law, attempted to enter the office premises. PW1
testified that the Accused-Appellant prevented them from entering the premises.
Consequently, PW1 lodged a complaint with the Criminal Investigation Department
(CID) in relation to the incident.
28. During cross-examination, the defence failed to mark any material contradiction or
omission in the evidence of PW1. On the contrary, PW1 remained consistent in his
testimony throughout the trial and maintained the same account of the sequence of
events.
29. It is significant that PW1 had reposed a considerable degree of trust and confidence in
the Accused-Appellant. The evidence of PW1 was that such trust was dishonestly
abused by the Accused-Appellant for his own benefit.
“ප්‍ර: ඒ එවන ලද කාරණයක් එහි සදහන් වවලා නැහැ?
9 | P a g e
උ: කරණය 7% මිල මුළු ප්‍රමාණය 7% මිල ආපහු කම්පනියට දන්නා එව්වව්. ඉතින් ඒක
මුල ඉදලා ඔය ව ෝඩ් මිටින් ඒක දවවසේ ඉදලම මුල ඉදලම හදල තිවයන්න සල්ලි ගන්න
වුවමනාවවන් කරලා තිවයන්වන්. ඉතින් මන් වකාවහාමද ඕව දන්වන්. මම හිතුවා වම්
විසේවාශ කරන්න ඕන කියල. මට කිව්වව් වලායර්සේලට අඩ්වයිසේ කරන එක්වකවනක්.
ලන්ඩන්වල එම්.ඒ. කරපු එක්වකවනක්, හියුමන් රයිට්සේ වලෝයර් වකවනක් කියල මට
කිව්වව්. ඉතින් මම ඊට වැඩිය වමාකක්ද මනුසේසවයක්වගන් ලාවපාරුත්තතු වවන්වන්.” (at
vide page 164 of the Appeal Brief)
30. The next material witness called on behalf of the prosecution was PW5, a Chartered
Accountant. According to his evidence, PW5 initially acted as an income tax consultant
to PW1 and subsequently undertook auditing work in respect of PW1’s land.
31. Thereafter, by letter dated 04.09.2009, PW1 appointed PW5 as the auditor of
Hakwatuna Oya Resorts Pvt Ltd for the purpose of conducting an audit of the affairs of
the company. According to the evidence of PW5, the audit was undertaken following
the emergence of certain issues between the alternative directors of the company, and
the appointment was made at the request of the Accused-Appellant.
32. During the course of the said audit, PW5 discovered certain irregularities and
malpractices on the part of Kariyawasam. It was further revealed that the accounts of
the company had not been properly maintained and that certain vouchers had not been
duly signed. Following these findings, Kariyawasam agreed to repay to PW1 a sum of
Rs. 2,4725,000/- in respect of the monies alleged to have been misappropriated.
Accordingly, upon the completion of the preliminary audit conducted by PW5,
Kariyawasam repaid the said sum to PW1. Thereafter, at the request of PW1,
Kariyawasam resigned from his position as an alternative director of the company.
33. Following the resignation of Kariyawasam, PW1 entrusted the Accused-Appellant with
the responsibility of attending to the affairs and tasks relating to the next stage of the
hotel project. At the same time, PW1 appointed PW2 as a new alternative director of
the said company, alongside the Accused-Appellant.
10 | P a g e
34. Accordingly, the Accused-Appellant and PW2 entered into an agreement whereby PW2
was to attend to the financial transactions of the company, under the supervision and
oversight of the Accused-Appellant. It was further agreed that the Accused-Appellant
and PW2 would be entitled, collectively, to 10% of the profits arising from the hotel
project.
“ප්‍ර: දැන් විත්තතිකරු විසින් කරන ලද වසේවාව වවනුවවන් ඔහුට යම්කිසි මුදලක් වගවීමට
වපාවරාන්ු වවලා තිබුනද මහත්තමයාවේ දැනුම හැටියට?
උ: මවේ දැනුවම් හැටියට සහ වඩාක්ටර් නිහාල්ල නානායක්කාර මට පවසල තිවයන විදියට
වැටුප් වගවීමක් සම් න්ධවයන් දැනුම් දීමක් කරලා නැහැ. ඒ සදහා ඒ වයාපෘති වලට මුදල්ල
උඔදවන ඇත්තතන්ට වපාවරාන්ු වවලා තිවයන්වන් එම සමාගවම් වකාටසේ ල ා දීම. ඔය
වයාපෘතිවේ සෑම පිරිවයකින්ම ආවයෝජනවයන් 10% ක ප්‍රමාණයක් වකාටසේ ල ා දීම

58. Accordingly, the contention advanced by the Accused-Appellant cannot be sustained
when the evidence as a whole is considered. The issue is not merely whether the
Accused-Appellant devoted his time and professional expertise to the project without
receiving a conventional salary. Rather, the material question is the nature and purpose
of the monies entrusted to him and whether he was entitled to deal with those monies
as his own.
59. The evidence establishes that the Accused-Appellant engaged in the project pursuant to
an arrangement whereby he was to be entitled to a 7% share in the company in
consideration of the services rendered by him. However, there is no agreement
providing for the payment of a salary or professional fees to the Accused-Appellant for
such services. On the contrary, the evidence was that the expenses and incidental costs
incurred by him in connection with the project were to be borne by the Hakwatuna Oya
company until the completion of the project.
19 | P a g e
60. It is also significant that the 8 invoices relied upon by the Accused-Appellant do not
exclusively relate to Hakwatuna Oya Resorts Pvt Ltd. Certain invoices were issued in
relation to Nilaweli Beach Resorts and Spa Pvt Ltd, notwithstanding the evidence that
the latter company had not commenced substantive financial transactions or activities
at the relevant time. These circumstances materially undermine the proposition that the
monies paid pursuant to those invoices represented genuine professional fees for
services rendered to Hakwatuna Oya Resorts Pvt Ltd.
61. Furthermore, the evidence regarding the actual movement and subsequent utilization of
the monies is inconsistent with the assertion that the entire amount of AUD 108,500
was paid to the Accused-Appellant as professional remuneration. The evidence
demonstrates that the monies were entrusted to him in connection with the investment
in the hotel project and the acquisition of his agreed 7% shares in the company.
However, portions of those funds were subsequently transferred between his personal
accounts, utilized towards the settlement of a bank overdraft, and placed in fixed
deposits.
62. Accordingly, the aforesaid contention of the Accused-Appellant is devoid of merit and
cannot be sustained on the evidence. The totality of the evidence establishes the nature
and purpose of the monies entrusted to the Accused-Appellant and does not support the
assertion that the said monies were paid to him as professional fees. Therefore, the said
ground of appeal must necessarily fail.
63. In this regard, the following authorities further elaborate the essential ingredients
required to establish the offence of criminal breach of trust;
64. In Attorney General Vs. Dewapriya Walgamage and Another (1990) 2 Sri. L.R. 212,
held that;
“If the initial taking could be only an irregularity of procedure or would not
constitute theft or cheating, the accused could be found guilty of criminal
misappropriation or criminal breach of trust. The correct test is to ascertain
whether the accused is guilty of another offence such as cheating or theft at the time
of the initial taking.”
20 | P a g e
“I have already held that the evidence in the case does not in any way warrant an
inference that the accused was guilty of the offence of cheating at the time of the
initial taking of the property. In these circumstances I see no merit in the
submissions made by Counsel for the Accused-Appellant. I accordingly uphold the
conviction of the Accused-Appellant.”
65. In Basnayake Vs. Officer-in-Charge of Special Crimes Detection Unit,
Anuradhapura (1988) 2 Sri. L.R. 50, held that;
“The inference of dishonest misappropriation or conversion is an essential
ingredient of the offence under Section 391 of the Penal Code.”
66. In Kalyanaratne Vs. Gunadasa 40 NLR 44, held that;
“It is submitted on behalf of the appellant that his liability is civil only since he
received the Rs. 5, if he did receive it, by virtue of the promissory note which was
made out to him, and Gunadasa was liable in law to discharge his obligation to the
appellant, and the appellant only, who thus received the money in his own legal
right. But I think the terms of section 388 of the Penal Code are sufficiently wide to
cover a case of this kind, and illustration (a) to this section certainly indicates one
instance where the legal owner of property can commit criminal breach of trust in
respect of it. If that were not so, many cases of misappropriation by servants and
agents of the property for which they are bound to account to their employers would
go unpunished. This case does in fact bear a sufficiency of resemblance to the King
Vs. Perera, where Jayewardena A.J. upheld the conviction for criminal breach of
trust of a salesman who misappropriated cheques made out in his own name by
purchasers of his employer’s goods.”
67. The principles set out in the aforesaid authorities are directly applicable to the present
case. The evidence establishes that the monies were entrusted to the Accused-Appellant
pursuant to an agreement for a specific purpose, namely, to be utilized in connection
with the investment in Hakwatuna Oya Resorts (Pvt) Ltd and the acquisition of his
agreed 7% shares in the project. The Accused-Appellant was therefore not placed in
possession of the monies with unrestricted right to deal with them as his own. His
21 | P a g e
obligation was to utilize the funds in accordance with the arrangement between the
parties.
68. The evidence, however, demonstrates a departure from that agreed purpose. Instead of
applying the monies towards the intended investment, the Accused-Appellant
transferred substantial sums between his personal bank accounts, utilized part of the
funds to settle a personal bank overdraft and subsequently placed monies in fixed
deposits. These transactions cannot reasonably be regarded as acts done in furtherance
of the investment for which the funds had been entrusted and thereby breached the
arrangement pursuant to which the monies had been entrusted to him.
69. In these circumstances, the subsequent use of the entrusted funds for his own financial
affairs cannot be justified merely by referring to the services he had rendered to the
company as contended by the Appellant. As recognized in the aforesaid authorities,
even where a person asserts a personal right or interest in property, criminal breach of
trust may arise where the property was entrusted to him for a particular purpose and he
dishonestly deals with it otherwise.
70. The circumstances therefore provide a sufficient basis for the inference of dishonest
misappropriation or conversion required for the offence of criminal breach of trust. The
authorities cited above, when applied to the facts of the present case, support the
conclusion that the Accused-Appellant dishonestly converted monies entrusted to him
for his own use.
71. Moreover, it is relevant to note that, on 27.04.2022, the Appellant made an application
to this Court under Section 351(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, seeking to
adduce as fresh evidence an audit report marked A1. The said report had originally been
produced by the same virtual complainant in the District Court Case No. DMR
72. By order dated 26.01.2026, this Court allowed the application and admitted the said
audit report into the record as fresh evidence. Relying upon the contents of A1, the
Appellant has sought to challenge the evidentiary value of the audit report dated
09.12.20210, marked P12, which relates to Hakwatuna Oya Resorts Pvt Ltd. It is
22 | P a g e
contended that P12 covered only a period of approximately 6 months and 19 days and
is therefore incomplete, whereas A1 purportedly constituted the audit report covering
the company’s full financial year. The Appellant further contended that the learned High
Court Judge placed substantial reliance upon P12, particularly upon its purported
finding that the sum of AUD 108,500 remained unsettled or unaccounted for by the
Appellant. However, it is contended that no corresponding entry appears in A1
indicating that the said sum was unaccounted for.
73. On that basis, the Appellant contended that the prosecution, despite the alleged
availability of A1, failed to produce the said report during the High Court trial. The
Appellant therefore contended that the non-production of A1 ought to give rise to an
adverse inference against the prosecution pursuant to Section 114(f) of the Evidence
Ordinance, particularly since, according to the Appellant, the contents of A1 materially
differ from the matters relied upon in P12.
74. It is pertinent to observe, however, that the prosecution case did not rest upon either the
audit report marked P12 or the audit report subsequently admitted as fresh evidence and
marked A1. The conviction of the Appellant was not founded upon the alleged finding
in P12 that the sum of AUD 108,500 remained unsettled and uncounted for. The fact
that P12 covered a limited period, and the Appellant’s contention that A1 constituted a
subsequent and more comprehensive audit, therefore, does not by itself affect the
essential foundation of the prosecution case. Moreover, as the author of A1, namely
PW5, is deceased and was consequently unavailable to give evidence regarding the
preparation and contents of the said report, the evidentiary significance that may
properly be attached to A1 must also be considered in that context.
75. More importantly, the evidence of the prosecution witness independently establishes
that the sum of AUD 108,500 was remitted to and deposited in the personal bank
account of the Appellant. The evidence further establishes the purpose for which those
monies were entrusted to him, namely to be utilized in connection with the investment
in Hakwatuna Oya Resorts Pvt Ltd., in accordance with the arrangement between the
parties. This evidence does not depend upon the findings contained in P12.
23 | P a g e
76. In this regard, there is no evidence of any agreement pursuant to which the Appellant
was entitled to receive the said AUD 10,50 as salary or professional fees. On the
contrary, the evidence establishes that his entitlement under the arrangement between
the parties was in respect of the agreed share in the project, while the expenses and
incidental costs relating to the project were to be borne by the company. Then, the
subsequent utilization of the monies for his own financial purposes must therefore be
considered against the specific purpose for which the funds had been entrusted to him.
77. Accordingly, the non-production of the audit report marked A1 and its contents do not
affect the evidence establishing the entrustment of the monies to the Accused-
Appellant. Since the prosecution case is supported by the testimonies of the prosecution
witnesses and other documentary evidence independently of P12, the reliance placed
by the Appellant on A1 does not create any reasonable doubt as to the finding of
dishonest misappropriation of the said monies by the learned High Court Judge. The
said contention advanced by the Appellant is therefore devoid of merit and must fail.
78. Further, the Accused-Appellant has argued that he was denied a fair trial before the
High Court. However, the proceedings recorded in the High Court do not support such
a contention. The trial commenced in November 2013 and continued until January
2018, during which period the Accused-Appellant was represented by several counsel
at different stages of the proceedings.
79. It is further apparent that, at a certain stage, the Accused-Appellant, being himself an
Attorney-at-Law, elected to conduct the case personally. The learned High Court Judge
nevertheless afforded him the same facilities and opportunities that would ordinarily
have been extended to a counsel appearing for the defence. Moreover, when the
Accused-Appellant sought an adjournment in order to obtain the assistance of senior
counsel, the learned High Court Judge acceded to his request. Significantly, when the
matter was thereafter taken up for the defence case, the Accused-Appellant was once
again represented by Counsel of his choice.

80. In Attorney General Vs. Segulebbe Latheef and Another, (2008) 1 S.L.R. 225, J.A.N.
De Silva, J., held that,
“The right of an accused person to a fair trial is recognized in all the criminal
justice systems in the civilized world. Its denial is generally proof enough that
justice is denied.”
“Like the concept of fairness, a fair trial is also not capable of a clear definition.
The right to a fair trial amongst other things includes the following;
i. The equality of all persons before the court.
ii. A fair and public hearing by a competent, independent and impartial
court/tribunal established by law.
iii. Presumption of innocence until guilt is proven according to law.
iv. The right of an accused person to be informed or promptly and in detail in a
language he understands of the nature and cause of the charge against him.
v. The right of an accused to have time and facilities for preparation for the trial.
vi. The right to have a counsel and to communicate with him.
vii. The right of an accused to be tried without much delay.
viii. The right of an accused to be tried in his presence and to defend himself or
through counsel.
ix. The accused has a right to be informed of his rights.
x. If the accused is in indigent circumstances to provide legal assistance without
any charge from the accused.
xi. The right of an accused to examine or have examined the witnesses against him
and to obtain the evidence and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the
same conditions as witnesses against him.
xii. If the accused cannot understand or speak the language in which proceedings
are conducted to have the assistance of an interpreter.
xiii. The right of an accused not to be compelled to testify against himself or to
confess guilty.
81. In these circumstances, the High Court proceedings demonstrate that the Accused-
Appellant was afforded adequate and repeated opportunities to obtain legal

representation and to present his defence, and there is no basis to conclude that he was
deprived of a fair trial or that any prejudice was caused to him in the conduct of the
proceedings.
82. In view of the foregoing analysis of the grounds of appeal and the impugned judgment,
I find no reason to interfere with the findings of the Learned High Court Judge.
Accordingly, I affirm the conviction and sentence imposed by the Learned Trial Judge.
Consequently, the appeal is dismissed.
